title: Screwworm Monitoring Camera Gap: What Landowners Miss at Trap Sites
content:
A screwworm monitoring camera can show what uses a trap site when cattle checks cover only the managed herd. Landowners can tighten cattle checks during a New World screwworm alert and still leave another part of the property unseen. Feral hog lines and wildlife crossings may stay active at night. Trap sites may have no regular inspection. That is the screwworm monitoring gap.

A screwworm monitoring camera does not diagnose parasites. It closes a visibility hole. The mobile hosts on that line are otherwise hard to inspect. Per USDA APHIS, screwworm targets live, warm-blooded animals with fresh wounds, not feces. If you suspect a case, contact USDA APHIS and your state agricultural extension office for confirmation and reporting.

Where the Monitoring Gap Appears

Cattle are visible, handled, and usually covered by a routine. Feral hogs and other wildlife are different. They move through brush and fence gaps, fight, pick up fresh cuts, and return to bait or water when nobody is at the property. A weekly trap drive can show what happened days ago, but it cannot show what moved through the site last night.

Trap lines are useful observation points. You already place them where hogs concentrate. Fresh rooting, trails, wallows, bait, and water bring animals back to a predictable area. The same site can show which sounders are using the property. It can show whether activity is increasing and whether a catch changed pressure on the line.

What a Trap-Site Camera Can Do

A wild hog trap camera system is built for trap operations first. Live video lets you count hogs and read commitment. It also shows the area inside and outside the trap before you send a closure command. During a biosecurity alert, that same view provides useful movement context without pretending to be a veterinary tool.

  • Show when feral hogs are active at a monitored site
  • Help distinguish hog activity from other wildlife at the bait edge
  • Support whole-sounder removal by showing when the group is committed
  • Reduce unnecessary drives to quiet or empty traps

The camera cannot confirm screwworm. It cannot identify larvae from video. It does not replace wound checks or agency reporting. Observation supports awareness. USDA APHIS and extension partners handle confirmation and response.

Build a Trap-Line Observation Layer

Start with the primary baited trap where you are conditioning or catching a sounder. Add a secondary crossing or shared water edge if activity shifts away from the main site. Mount the camera so you can see the trap entrance, the area inside the trap, and the approach path. The trapping decision comes first. The added wildlife visibility comes from the same frame.

A purpose-built HogEye steel camera is designed for trap-site durability and live reads. Keep a simple log with the date, site, sounder estimate, catch outcome, and unusual activity. The camera resources library can support installation and field checks.

Use Monitoring to Improve Capture Timing

Remote monitoring and trapping are one workflow. Watch the live feed. Wait until the full sounder is inside and settled. Then trigger the gate when the closure criteria are met. A partial capture educates survivors and can push them into a crossing you are not watching. Seeing the catch happen gives your team evidence about whether removal worked and whether another sounder replaced the first.

During an alert season, assign one person to review active feeds each morning. Assign a backup to send closure commands. Keep USDA APHIS and extension contacts in the same team channel as trap alerts. In slower periods, maintain a lighter health check. A dark camera should not reopen the blind spot.

Practical Next Steps

  • List the trap sites where feral hogs already concentrate
  • Confirm each camera reports from the final mount location
  • Review active sites before scheduling a drive
  • Log sounder activity even when no catch occurs
  • Report suspected screwworm without waiting for camera evidence

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a screwworm monitoring camera diagnose an infestation?

No. It supports observation and trap decisions only. Contact USDA APHIS and your state extension office if you suspect screwworm.

Why focus on trap sites?

Trap sites are where feral hogs already concentrate, so one camera can close a high-value visibility gap without covering every acre.

Does screwworm breed in manure?

No. USDA APHIS describes screwworm as a threat to live animals with fresh wounds, not feces. Maggots in waste are a different fly.
